childMarkdownRemark.html:
Project overview

  • Project type: Commercial mobile application UI/UX overhaul (migrated from the Spring-A-Story web platform to React Native).
  • Target audience: Dual user base — early-stage emergent readers aged 2 to 6, and parents/educators tracking educational progress.
  • Team setup: Solo project, owning end-to-end product discovery, interaction design, information architecture, and UI execution.
  • Core skills demonstrated: Child-centred UX research, pedagogical game mechanics, accessibility design (WCAG compliance for motor/cognitive constraints), component-based design systems, rapid wireframing, and multi-device interaction prototyping.

What this project proves about me: I design complex digital experiences tailored to extreme usability constraints—transforming pedagogical learning theory and technical product requirements into intuitive, accessible, and delightful mobile interfaces.

The challenge

Early-childhood literacy digital tools frequently suffer from one of two product failure modes: they are either passive content streams (mimicking static videos with zero interactive reinforcement) or heavily cluttered interfaces that trigger severe cognitive overload for developing minds.

Building upon longitudinal insights gathered from the predecessor web platform, Spring-A-Story, the objective was to design a commercial-grade, multi-platform React Native application specifically structured for pre-readers and early readers aged 2 to 6.

The core design challenges included:

  1. Severe physical and cognitive constraints: Children in this developmental bracket lack fine motor control, cannot parse dense textual instructions, and possess short attention spans.
  2. The dual-persona friction: Balancing autonomous, safe exploration for the child against granular performance tracking and security gating for parents.
  3. Pedagogical efficacy: Embedding phonological awareness, active reading validation, and positive reinforcement loops without making the experience feel like an exam or creating screen-time fatigue.

My process

I followed an iterative, human-centred product design methodology adapted for early childhood education:

  1. Strategic discovery & pedagogical requirements: Synthesised web legacy data, documented child usability principles, and established a 7-tier reading difficulty framework.
  2. Functional planning & MoSCoW prioritisation: Defined MVP (Minimum Viable Product) feature scope, gamification mechanics (Mastery Points), and parental oversight architecture.
  3. Information architecture & user flows: Mapped touch-based navigation paths, safety-gated flows, and horizontal story layouts.
  4. Low-fidelity exploration & sketches: Iterated screen layouts on paper and low-fi digital wireframes to validate spatial relationships and touch target scaling.
  5. Design system & high-fidelity prototyping: Built reusable modular UI components in Adobe XD, applied accessible typography and high-contrast palettes, and specified micro-interactions.
  6. Validation planning & technical handoff: Defined tracking parameters for parental diagnostics ("Struggle Words") and structured component assets for React Native implementation.

What I did

1. Strategic Discovery & Product Roadmapping

I initiated the project by mapping out user research insights into core developmental requirements. Unlike adult interfaces where utility and speed govern usability, child interfaces demand multisensory confirmation, extreme visual clarity, and low cognitive noise.

I translated child developmental psychology into three core product pillars:

  • Phonetic recognition: Providing visual-to-auditory alignment so text sounds match visible word shapes.
  • Engagement loops: Rewarding effort rather than absolute accuracy to encourage resilience.
  • Child accessibility standards: Accommodating gross motor gestures (flat-palm tapping, dragging) rather than fine tap accuracy.

Qualitative research synthesis categorising child usability considerations and pedagogical reading strategies into actionable UX guidelines.

I structured the MVP feature scope using a MoSCoW (Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have) prioritisation matrix. I prioritised real-time audio playback, phoneme-highlight synchronization, and haptic feedback as essential P0 features. To structure educational progression, I designed a seven-level tiered difficulty roadmap driven by "Mastery Points" and a star-based scoring engine.

Early functional planning outlining the star reward logic, metadata structure for storybooks, and a 7-tier reading difficulty framework.

2. Interaction Design & Layout Architecture

During layout planning, I focused on reducing cognitive friction. I engineered an explicit separation between the child's active reading zone and adult administration.

  • Motor skill touch zones: Standard 44x44px touch targets were replaced with oversized touch regions (minimum 72x72px equivalent) and generous boundary padding to accommodate clumsy grip postures on tablets.
  • Audio-visual synchronisation ("Follow-the-Bounce"): Designed an automated text-tracking state machine where active words scale dynamically and change colour in sync with voice narration.
  • Safety-first parental gating: All account configurations, subscription screens, and external links were placed behind arithmetic or adult gesture gates to protect accidental checkout and privacy compliance.

Initial annotated wireframes exploring touch controls, drawing canvas utilities, and adult parental oversight mechanisms.

Low-fidelity digital tablet wireframes mapping key flows: story selection grid, interactive reading canvas, creative drawing, and audio review.

3. Iterative Prototyping & Flow Simplification

Moving from conceptual diagrams to paper sketches allowed me to test layout orientations rapidly. I explored horizontal versus vertical reading orientations, concluding that a landscape, horizontal page-turn mental model most effectively mirrored physical books and prepared children for print literacy.

  • Cognitive load reduction: Stripped all non-essential UI indicators during reading sessions—removing battery percentages, system clocks, and ambient navigation menus.
  • Drawing and interaction spaces: Integrated tactile activities within story breaks, allowing children to colour scenes or trace letterforms to reinforce muscle memory.

Notebook ideation sketches detailing layout options, narrative flow transitions, and interactive drawing interactions.

4. High-Fidelity Execution & Design System

In Adobe XD, I created a component-driven design system engineered for visual clarity, emotional delight, and cross-platform consistency across tablet and mobile displays.

  • Accessible typography: Selected clear, rounded letterforms that clearly distinguish ambiguous glyphs (such as lowercase 'l', uppercase 'I', and numeral '1') to support early readers and neurodiverse children.
  • Visual reward micro-interactions: Designed high-contrast celebratory states using star explosions and character animations to celebrate page milestones.
  • State management: Documented states for Default, Active Reading, Struggle/Retry, and Success to guide the child intuitively without inducing frustration or requiring adult correction.

Comprehensive high-fidelity screen flows covering onboarding, profile switching, story categorisation, interactive reading, and reward overlays.

Why I made these decisions

  1. Horizontal landscape orientation over vertical scroll: Toddlers and early learners find continuous vertical scrolling disorienting. A discrete, horizontal paginated model mimics real-world books, establishing a clear beginning, middle, and end per screen.
  2. Persistent multi-modal feedback (Visual + Audio + Haptic): Pre-literate children rely heavily on sensory confirmation. Combining audible phonics with visual scaling and subtle device vibration ensures immediate reinforcement, accommodating various learning speeds.
  3. Decoupled parent dashboard with struggle-word telemetry: Instead of interrupting reading sessions with performance grades, struggle metrics are silently captured in the background. Parents access these insights inside a gated portal to review specific phonetic hesitations without diminishing the child's reading confidence.
  4. Restricted in-reading UI chrome: Removing system-level controls during the story prevents accidental taps from breaking immersion or closing the application, significantly reducing child frustration.

Impact / results

While developed as an end-to-end prototype and product specification for React Native implementation, the project achieved several foundational milestones:

Area Operational & Product Outcome
Product Architecture Consolidated legacy web features into an efficient mobile design system featuring 20+ reusable components tailored for React Native.
Pedagogical Alignment Successfully established a 7-tier difficulty taxonomy paired with automated star-gated progression logic.
Child Usability Standards Validated zero-text visual navigation patterns, enabling pre-readers to independently launch stories and engage with interactive narration.
Parental Gating Security Implemented a 100% gated separation between learning canvases and account/settings panels to eliminate accidental actions.

Usability validation framework

The resulting high-fidelity prototype was prepared for cohort testing with parents and children to validate three key UX metrics:

  • Story completion rate: Evaluating whether children finish chosen titles without abandoning the flow.
  • Phonemic struggle recovery: Assessing how seamlessly children recover after encountering unfamiliar words using the "Follow-the-Bounce" feature.
  • Autonomous navigation: Measuring whether children aged 3–5 can navigate from the home screen into a story without parental intervention.

Tools and skills applied

Category Tools / skills
Design & Prototyping Adobe XD, Paper Prototyping, Wireframing, Component Libraries, Design Systems
UX & Pedagogical Research Early-Childhood UX, Accessibility (WCAG), MoSCoW Prioritisation, Gamification Architecture
Platform & Tech Strategy React Native UI Specifications, Cross-Device Responsive Layouts (Mobile & Tablet)
Product Management Feature Prioritisation, Educational Roadmapping, Telemetry & Metric Specification

Roles performed on this project

  • Product Owner: Defined product scope, feature prioritisation, educational difficulty architecture, and parental dashboard analytics.
  • UX Designer: Researched early-childhood accessibility, mapped intuitive multi-modal flows, wireframed touch targets, and conducted layout iterations.
  • UI / Visual Designer: Developed the high-fidelity design system, iconography, palette guidelines, and reward micro-interaction states in Adobe XD.

childMarkdownRemark.excerpt: End-to-end UX/UI design and product architecture for a gamified, accessible React Native children's literacy app for ages 2 to 6.

childMarkdownRemark.html: Translating the existing Spring-A-Story web application into a commercially viable, cross-platform React Native product required solving a dual-user problem: early learners (ages 2–6) with developing motor skills, and parents seeking transparent literacy progress without screen-time guilt. Acting as solo Product Owner and UX/UI Designer, I developed an end-to-end pedagogical reading experience grounded in phoneme recognition, gamified retention loops, and child-safe interface patterns. Through rapid paper prototyping, low-fidelity wireframing, and an accessible high-fidelity design system in Adobe XD, I designed large touch targets, horizontal digital storytelling mimics, gated parental settings, and interactive feedback mechanisms. The resulting design specifications established a scalable, multi-level reading progression framework ready for engineering delivery and cohort usability testing.
